title: Kill your darlings
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Brien argues that teachers and schools need to be willing to cut cherished practices, borrowing the editor's maxim to kill your darlings. He uses a long anecdote about being nearly cut from a reality TV show for refusing to reshape his story, then applies the lesson to teaching: lessons built around the teacher's effort are about the teacher, not the students. Drawing on The Pruning Principle, he proposes addition by strategic subtraction, such as replacing collected exit passes with mini whiteboards to save hours of marking. He argues that schools add initiatives without removing anything, and that leaders must model and repeatedly return to any change. He closes by crediting stripping out engaging activities for better-than-predicted results in his classes.
points: Attachment to self-created resources and routines makes change feel like loss, and 'I've always done it this way' signals a lesson that is about the teacher.
Pruning tasks by rating time taken against value added frees teacher time, as with mini whiteboards replacing marking.
Schools overload staff by adding initiatives without removing anything, which guarantees haphazard implementation.
Shared high-quality resource banks could save teachers many hours a year spent creating materials.
Change sticks only when leaders model it consistently and keep referring back to it, and resistant teachers need a one-to-one conversation.
quotes: Change isn’t easy, but it is often necessary. I want to spend some time exploring why when approached thoughtfully, change is good.
This refers to the words, stories or paragraphs you’ve created that you love and have an attachment to, but are actually adding little to no value to the final product.
These lessons (despite the teachers good intentions are not about the student, they are about the teacher and the efforts they have put in to creating them).

They highlight the importance of analyzing all of the tasks that we do inside and outside of the classroom as educators and rate how much time they take versus how much value they are actually adding. Insanity is repeating the same process again and again and expecting different results, yet sometimes we are so married to the ways we have always done things that we refuse to change. When we’re able to take a Birds Eye view at what we are spending all of our time on, it makes it easier to remove those things that are honestly actually a waste of your expertise.

Oftentimes when schools introduce new initiatives, despite the best of intentions, they are adding on to staff workload without taking anything away. No matter how good the initiative is, if staff are already at capacity it is not going to be implemented effectively as staff spread themselves too thin and either avoid the change all together or implement a haphazard version of it with limited enthusiasm.

To kill my darlings of all of these ‘engaging activities’ I’ve been able to get to a point in my career where if we look at our data over 80% students are achieving better than predicted at a VCE level showing that changing and focusing on only the teaching strategies proven to add value saves me time and helps to achieve our overarching goal which is providing the students with the opportunities to pursue their desired pathway.
